title: Design Review — Mobile Onboarding
description: Walkthrough of the shortened signup flow, edge cases and instrumentation.
transcript: Right, I think we're all here. This is going to be a long one, so I'll try to move quickly and we can go deep where it matters.
The goal today is to get the mobile onboarding flow to a state where David can build it without coming back to me every twenty minutes.
That's a low bar, to be fair. I ask a lot of questions.
You ask good questions. That's why we're doing this properly.
I'm mostly here to listen, but I'll jump in if I think we're scoping something into Q4 by accident.
Please do. Okay — context first, for anyone who's come to this cold.
The current signup is four steps. Email and password, then verify, then workspace name, then invite your team.
We lose about forty percent of people between step two and step three.
Forty percent is enormous. Is that mobile specifically or across the board?
Mobile specifically. On desktop it's closer to fifteen.
That gap is suspicious. Same flow, very different drop-off.
It is, and that's actually the interesting part. We dug into it and the problem isn't the number of steps, it's the verify step.
On mobile you have to leave the app, go to your email client, find the code, and come back.
And on the way back a lot of people just don't.
Exactly. The session's still alive, the account exists, but they never return.
So the fix isn't fewer steps, it's not making people leave the app.
Right. Fewer steps is a consequence, not the goal.
That reframes it a lot. I'd assumed we were just compressing screens.
That was the original brief and I think it was wrong. Let me show you what I've got instead.
Screen one — email address only. No password field at all.
Magic link, with a code fallback. You enter your email, we send a link, tapping the link brings you straight back into the app.
On mobile that works nicely because the link opens the app directly if it's installed.
What happens if the app isn't installed? Which for a new signup is the common case.
Then it opens the web app, and we prompt to install afterwards rather than before.
Okay, that's the deferred-deep-link problem. It's solvable but it's genuinely fiddly.
How fiddly? That's exactly the kind of thing I want to know now.
The mechanism itself is fine. The problem is that it behaves differently in every email client.
Gmail on iOS opens links in its own in-app browser, which doesn't trigger the app-open handoff.
So a Gmail-on-iPhone user — which is a lot of people — gets the web app even if they have the native app installed.
Correct. And they might not notice, which is arguably worse.
Sort of. We can detect the in-app browser reasonably reliably and show a 'open in app' banner. It's not elegant.
Is inelegant-but-working acceptable here, or does it undermine the whole idea?
I think it's acceptable. The failure mode is 'you're in the web app instead of the native app', which is a much smaller failure than 'you never came back'.
Then I'm fine with it. I just want it in the spec so it doesn't come back as a bug report.
What's the code fallback for? You mentioned it in passing.
Some corporate mail gateways rewrite links and break them. The code is a six-digit number in the same email that you can type in manually.
Good. That's the case that would otherwise generate support tickets nobody can reproduce.
How long is the code valid?
I've specified ten minutes. Is that reasonable?
Ten is fine. Fifteen is more forgiving but ten is defensible.
What happens at minute eleven? Does it say 'expired' or does it just fail?
It says expired, with a resend button that's already focused.
Good. The number of products that make you retype your email at that point is remarkable.
That was deliberate. We keep the email in state.
Screen two — and this is the only other screen — is workspace setup.
Workspace name, and an optional team invite that we've made genuinely optional rather than skippable-but-guilt-inducing.
What does that mean in practice?
The old design had 'Skip for now' in grey eight-point text at the bottom. The new one has 'Invite later' as a full-width secondary button.
Probably, slightly. But we're optimising for completed signups, and a user who bounces at the invite screen invites nobody at all.
That's the right trade. I just wanted to hear you say it out loud.
What's the workspace name prefilled with?
We derive it from the email domain. If you sign up as dana at acmecorp dot test, it prefills 'Acme Corp'.
Then we prefill nothing and use 'My workspace' as the placeholder.
You need a list of consumer domains for that. That list is never complete.
It doesn't need to be complete. Worst case someone gets 'Gmail' as a suggested workspace name and edits it.
I'd want the field focused with the text selected, so overwriting it is one action.
Okay. Let me walk the edge cases, because that's where these things fall apart.
Case one — the email already exists.
No. We send the magic link either way and the link logs them in rather than signing them up.
That's the right call for enumeration. You can't probe for which emails are registered.
It also means signup and login are the same flow, which halves the code.
What does the screen say after you submit? Because 'check your email' is different from 'we've sent you a link'.
'Check your inbox' with the email address shown, and an edit link in case they typed it wrong.
Good. The typo case is common and it's infuriating when you can't get back.
Case two — the link is opened on a different device from the one that requested it.
That's the one I was going to ask about. Request on your phone, open on your laptop.
We allow it. The link is bound to the account, not the device.
Somewhat. If someone forwards the email, the recipient gets in.
Which is true of every password reset email ever sent.
I'd still want the link single-use and short-lived. Ten minutes and one use.
Case three — the user abandons after screen one and comes back three days later.
The account half-exists at that point.
It does. My proposal is that we treat it as a fresh signup — new link, and they land on workspace setup because the email's already verified.
So the abandoned state is recoverable rather than a dead end.
Right. The worst outcome is someone who tries to sign up twice and gets told their email is taken by an account they can't access.
That's a real support ticket pattern. We get it monthly.
That's where I got the case from.
Case four — expired link, clicked anyway.
Lands on a page that says the link expired, with the email prefilled and a resend button. Two taps to recover.
What if they click an old link after already signing in?
Then we send them to the app. No error, no confusion.
Good. Showing an error to someone who is already logged in is a classic.
Case five, and this is the last one — offline.
Submitting the email with no connection?
Yes. The button goes into a loading state and then we need to fail gracefully.
How long before we give up?
On a bad mobile connection ten seconds is aggressive. Fifteen would produce fewer false failures.
And the message should say 'check your connection', not 'something went wrong'.
Agreed. Generic error copy is lazy.
That's the flow. David, does that give you enough to build from?
First — what does the loading state actually look like between tapping the link and landing in the app?
There's a splash with a spinner. It's in the file, I just didn't walk through it.
Fine. Second — is there any animation between screen one and screen two, or is it a hard cut?
Slide left, two hundred milliseconds. Same as the rest of the app.
Good, that's what I'd have done anyway.
Can I raise instrumentation before we finish?
We can't tell whether this worked unless we're measuring the same funnel we measured before.
Right now we track step transitions. If we go from four steps to two, the old funnel becomes meaningless.
That's a very good point and I'm glad you raised it now rather than in six weeks.
I'd want events on: email submitted, link sent, link opened, code used instead of link, workspace created, invite sent, invite skipped.
Link opened is the interesting one. That's the number that tells us whether the whole premise holds.
Exactly. If link-opened is still forty percent below email-submitted, we've moved the problem rather than solved it.
Can you write that up as a spec? I'd rather it be your list than my approximation of your list.
Yes, I'll do that this week.
One question from me. What's the rollback if this performs worse?
The old flow doesn't go away immediately, so we can flag between them.
How long do we keep both?
I'd say two weeks of data, then delete the old one. Carrying two signup flows indefinitely is how you end up with neither working.
Two weeks is fine. Put a date on it so it actually gets deleted.
I'll put a ticket in with the date.
Accessibility — has this been through a screen reader pass?
Not yet. It's designed with it in mind but it hasn't been tested.
I'd want that before it ships rather than after. The code entry field especially — six separate inputs is usually a disaster with a screen reader.
It's one input, not six boxes.
Oh, good. That solves most of it.
The six-box pattern also breaks paste on half of Android.
Then I'll do a screen reader pass once there's something to test.
I want to name something before we close. This has slipped twice already.
I'm not looking for an explanation, I'm looking for a date I can defend to the board.
If I start Monday, internal testing by the end of the month is realistic. Not certain, realistic.
The deferred deep link. If that turns out to be worse than I think, it could eat a week.
Can you spike it first? Two days, just to find out.
That's a good idea. I'd know by Wednesday whether the date holds.
Then do that, and tell me Wednesday. I'd rather have bad news early.
Okay. To recap — I'll finalise the spec with the fifteen-second timeout and the offline copy.
David spikes the deep link Monday and Tuesday, reports Wednesday.
Nina writes the instrumentation spec this week and does a screen reader pass once there's a build.
That's a good session. Thanks Priya, that was a lot more thorough than the last one.
The last one was rushed. This is what happens when you get an extra week.

summary.overview: Mobile signup loses roughly forty percent of users between verification and workspace setup, against fifteen percent on desktop. The diagnosis is that the gap is caused by forcing users out of the app to fetch a verification code, not by the number of steps — so the redesign is passwordless magic-link with a code fallback, collapsing signup to two screens. The team walked five edge cases and identified the deferred deep link as the main technical risk, particularly Gmail's in-app browser on iOS. Nina raised that the existing funnel instrumentation becomes meaningless under the new flow and will write a replacement spec. David will spike the deep link before committing to an end-of-month date.
summary.gist: Passwordless two-screen signup; deep-link handling is the schedule risk; funnel instrumentation must be rebuilt.

outline.title: Reframing: it is not the step count

notes.chapter: Reframing: it is not the step count
bullets: Mobile drop-off between verify and workspace setup is ~40%; desktop is ~15%.
Cause is leaving the app to retrieve a code, not the number of screens.
Fewer steps is a consequence of the fix, not the goal — the original brief had this backwards.
Gmail on iOS opens links in its own in-app browser, which defeats the app handoff.
Detectable and recoverable with an 'open in app' banner — inelegant but the failure mode is mild.
Accepted on the grounds that landing in the web app is far better than never returning.
Six-digit code covers corporate mail gateways that rewrite and break links.
Ten-minute expiry, single use; expiry screen keeps the email and focuses a resend button.
One input rather than six boxes — better for screen readers and for paste on Android.
Existing email: send the link regardless and log them in — no account enumeration, and signup and login become one flow.
Cross-device open is permitted; the link is bound to the account, single use, ten minutes.
Abandoned signup is recoverable rather than a dead end — a known monthly support pattern.
Clicking an expired or stale link while already signed in sends the user to the app, not an error.
Offline submit times out at fifteen seconds with 'check your connection', not generic error copy.
The existing step-transition funnel becomes meaningless when four steps become two.
Required events: email submitted, link sent, link opened, code used, workspace created, invite sent, invite skipped.
Link-opened versus email-submitted is the number that says whether the premise holds at all.
Both flows behind a flag for two weeks of data, then the old one is deleted on a dated ticket.
Two-day spike on the deferred deep link before committing to end-of-month internal testing.

action_items.text: Finalise the onboarding spec with the 15s offline timeout and revised error copy
Spike the deferred deep link and report whether the end-of-month date holds
Write the funnel instrumentation spec for the new two-screen flow
Raise the dated ticket to delete the old signup flow after two weeks
Screen reader pass on the onboarding flow once a build exists
